question: What do the 12 basins look like (elevation, land cover), and do GIS statistics computed by us agree with the CAMELS attribute table?

outlines.note: shipped with CAMELS-US; hru_id = gauge id

elevation.product: 1-arc-second elevation tiles in SRTM .hgt format (Mapzen/Tilezen terrain tiles, AWS open data)
elevation.resolution: 1 arc-second, about 30 m; heights in whole metres
elevation.year: SRTM was flown in February 2000; the tile set was built in 2016-2017

land_cover.product: Annual NLCD land cover (USGS/MRLC), read from the USGS GeoServer that hosts the MRLC layers by WCS 1.0.0 GetCoverage
land_cover.resolution: 30 m, native grid in NAD83 / Conus Albers (EPSG:5070)

camels.note: area_gages2, elev_mean, slope_mean and frac_forest are listed in camels_attributes_v2.0.xlsx as 'N15 - USGS data' (Newman et al. 2015); the table gives neither the grid resolution nor the land-cover year behind them. dom_land_cover is from MODIS (IGBP classes).

methods.area: geodesic area of the outline on the GRS80 ellipsoid (pyproj.Geod); area_albers_km2 (planar area after projecting to an equal-area grid) and area_landcover_cells_km2 (30 m cells inside x 900 m2) are two cross-checks
methods.elevation: cells of the 1-arc-second grid whose centre lies inside the outline; the mean weights each cell by cos(latitude), i.e. by its true area
methods.slope: central differences on the 1-arc-second grid, with the cell size in metres computed per row from the latitude on the GRS80 ellipsoid; slope = 1000 x sqrt((dz/dx)^2 + (dz/dy)^2) in m per km, area-weighted mean over the basin. slope_mean_by_grid repeats this after averaging the grid over blocks of 3, 10 and 30 cells (elev_mean_by_grid likewise)
methods.shape: compactness_gravelius = perimeter / perimeter of a circle of equal area (1 = circle), with the perimeter of the outline smoothed to 100 m tolerance; elongation_ratio = diameter of a circle of equal area / longest straight line between two points of the outline (1 = circle, smaller = longer)
methods.land_cover: 30 m cells of the native Albers grid whose centre lies inside the outline (projected to the same grid); shares are cell counts, valid because the grid is equal-area. forest_share_1km_majority: the grid is cut into blocks of 33 x 33 cells (990 m), each block takes its most common group, and the share of the basin in 'forest' blocks is reported
methods.gauge: gauge position from CAMELS (gauge_lat, gauge_lon); distance_to_outline_km is the geodesic distance to the nearest point of the outline; elev_m is the elevation cell at the gauge
methods.comparison: difference = ours minus CAMELS (in % of the CAMELS value for area and slope); rank_correlation is Spearman's, over the 12 basins

basin_maps.caption: Elevation inside each basin outline, one row per landscape, basins ordered by size. Colours are stretched PER BASIN: light = the lowest point of that basin, dark = its highest point, and the range in metres is printed above each map. This shows the valleys of the flat Florida basins (a few tens of metres of relief) as clearly as those of the Appalachian basins (more than 1,000 m), but a colour does NOT mean the same height in two panels. Relief shading (light from the north-west) is added for texture; in low-relief basins it is exaggerated (factor 400 m / the basin's elevation range between its 2nd and 98th percentile, at most 12, on a smoothed grid), so shading strength must not be compared between panels either. North is up in every map; each panel has its own km scale bar; the white dot is the river gauge.

basin_landcover.caption: Land-cover groups in 2011 (Annual NLCD, 30 m) inside each outline; the line above each map names the two largest groups and their share. 'Farmland' is NLCD pasture/hay plus cultivated crops; 'built-up' is the four NLCD developed classes, which include roads and open developed land. North is up in every map; each panel has its own km scale bar; the white dot is the river gauge.

basin_gis_check.caption: Our statistics (vertical) against the CAMELS table (horizontal); a dot on the line means both agree. Area and slope use logarithmic axes. 'Typical' is the median over the 12 basins of ours minus CAMELS. In the slope panel the dots are the 30 m grid and the rings the same basins on the 920 m grid.

notes: Area: three ways of measuring the outline (geodesic, planar on the equal-area grid, counting 30 m cells) agree within 0.000%. Our area differs from the AREA field stored in the outline file by 0.000% on average, from CAMELS area_geospa_fabric by 0.09% (largest +1.0%, NE Cape Fear, NC) and from CAMELS area_gages2 by 0.7% (largest +3.8%, Hyco Creek, NC). area_gages2 comes from another data set (GAGES-II, with its own outline of the same basin), so a few percent there is a difference between sources, not an error of calculation.

Elevation: our mean differs from CAMELS elev_mean by +1.6 m in the median, but by more than 25 m in: Catawba, NC +47 m, French Broad, NC +100 m, South Toe, NC +163 m. Averaging our grid to coarser cells (up to 920 m) moves our mean by at most 2.5 m, so grid size does not explain this. The elev_mean field stored in the outline file is close to ours (mean absolute difference 8.4 m, largest -24.7 m, South Toe, NC). We cannot tell from the CAMELS documentation why its table is lower in these basins; the ranking of the basins is nearly the same (rank correlation 0.99) and the landscape classes of 01_data_audit.py (mountain = mean elevation above 600 m) are unchanged with our elevations.

Slope: on the 30 m grid our mean slope is +457% (median) against CAMELS slope_mean - several times steeper - with rank correlation 0.98. Slope depends strongly on the grid: 30 m: +457%, 90 m: +290%, 310 m: +136%, 920 m: +33% (median difference to CAMELS). The grid closest to CAMELS is 920 m, which suggests - but does not prove - that CAMELS slope_mean comes from a grid of about 1 km or coarser; its documentation does not say. The absolute value depends on the grid it is measured on. The model reads slope_mean after standardising it over the basins, so what matters to it is how the basins compare with one another, and their order is nearly the same.
In Charlie Creek, FL, Myakka, FL more than half of the 30 m cells have zero slope (heights are whole metres and the land is flat), so the mean slope there mostly reflects the 1 m steps of the data.

Forest: our forest share (NLCD deciduous + evergreen + mixed forest, 2011) is -11.3 percentage points against CAMELS frac_forest on average (mean absolute 12.4, largest -20.7, Little River, NC), rank correlation 0.98. Two possible reasons were tested. Definition: counting woody wetlands (forested swamps) as forest gives a mean absolute difference of 12.0 points - about as far from CAMELS as the plain forest share. Resolution: on a 990 m grid where every block takes its most common group the forest share is -2.7 points against CAMELS (mean absolute 6.7) - clearly closer to CAMELS than the 30 m share. It is not a full explanation: the coarse grid is closer to CAMELS in 8 of 12 basins and further away in the other 4, and its largest difference is -25.3 points (NE Cape Fear, NC). CAMELS does not document the land-cover map or year behind frac_forest; at 30 m, roads, clearings and pasture inside a forested basin are counted separately, which a coarser map cannot do.

Land cover is the 2011 layer of the yearly USGS land-cover series (Annual NLCD, same class codes as NLCD), not the older single-year 'NLCD 2011' release: www.mrlc.gov could not be reached through the proxy; the MRLC layers were read from the USGS GeoServer at dmsdata.cr.usgs.gov (workspaces named mrlc_...), where WCS 2.0.1 failed with a server error and WCS 1.0.0 worked. 2011 lies inside the study period (1980-2014); land cover is treated as fixed although it changed over 34 years.

Elevation tiles: the provider documents the tile set as a composite - SRTM (30 m) worldwide, with USGS 3DEP elevation used in the United States at finer zoom levels - and the tiles do not say which source a cell came from. We therefore call it '1-arc-second elevation in SRTM format', not pure SRTM.
Datum: outlines are NAD83, elevation tiles WGS84; the two differ by about a metre horizontally, far below the 30 m cell, so no datum shift was applied.

Outline detail: the outline vertices are 30 m apart on average, i.e. the outline follows the edges of 30 m raster cells. This staircase makes the raw perimeter 33% longer on average than the outline smoothed to 100 m, which is why the compactness uses the smoothed perimeter.

Outlines with more than one part: NE Cape Fear, NC (4 parts, largest 100.00% of the area); Charlie Creek, FL (6 parts, largest 100.00% of the area); Myakka, FL (2 parts, largest 100.00% of the area); SF Holston, VA (2 parts, largest 99.93% of the area). All parts are used.

Gauges: 12 of 12 gauges lie inside their outline, at most 0.63 km from its edge, and the elevation at the gauge is at most 12 m above the lowest cell of the basin: the outlets are where they should be.
Elevation voids inside the basins: 0 cells. Land-cover cells without a valid class: 0.0000% at most.

Land-cover groups: besides forest, shrub and grass, cropland and pasture, wetland, developed and water a seventh group, bare ground (NLCD 31, barren land), is kept so that the shares sum to 1; it is at most 1.0% of a basin (Myakka, FL). In the figure 'cropland and pasture' is labelled farmland and 'developed' is labelled built-up; the keys in this file keep the longer names.
The land-cover maps are resampled (nearest neighbour) to the elevation grid for drawing only; all shares come from the native 30 m Albers grid.
figures/basin_gis_check.png is an addition to the two figures named in the plan.
Nothing in this script is fitted, tuned or selected, so the train/validation/test split plays no role here.
